habit_line: Focus habit: Explain - Ask for the reason in the child's own words, said or written. Say: “How do you know? Tell it as if you were teaching a friend.” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome to the Fraction Frontier! Out here, fractions can be bigger than 1, and two fractions that look different can be the same size.
Today we build fractions with bars, line them up on number lines and find out which fraction is really bigger. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
do: Focus habit: Explain - Ask for the reason in the child's own words, said or written. Say: “How do you know? Tell it as if you were teaching a friend.” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: I will show you a fraction. Thumbs up if it is more than a half, thumbs down if it is less, flat hand if it is exactly a half.
Be ready to tell us HOW you know. A hint: what is half of the bottom number?
Each pizza has 4 slices. Ravi's group eats 11 slices. Is that more than 2 pizzas or less? More than 3? Write your guess before you build it.
stuck: Stuck: put 4 slices together. That is one whole pizza. How many whole pizzas can you make?
Not sure how to write it: "How many quarters did they eat? How many WHOLE pizzas and how many quarters left over?"
Finished early: what if every pizza had 6 slices and they ate 11 slices?

say: "7 thirds. 3 thirds make one whole, so I fill one bar: that uses 3. Another 3 fills a second bar. 1 third is left over. So 7/3 is 2 wholes and 1 third: 2 1/3. I can also say 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1."
"4 2/3 as thirds: each whole is 3 thirds, so 4 wholes are 12 thirds. Add the 2 thirds: 14 thirds, 14/3."
"3/5 of 30 stickers. The bottom number tells me how many equal units: 5. 5 units are 30, so 1 unit is 6. I need 3 units: 18."

do: Ask: "How many of these pieces make one whole?"
Ask: "Draw the bar. How many units? What is one unit worth?"
Ask: "Can you make the bottom numbers the same? Is it more or less than a half?"
stuck: Hint 1: "The denominator tells you how many pieces make one whole."
Hint 2: "For a fraction of a set, divide by the bottom number first, then multiply by the top number."
Hint 3: "To compare, change one fraction so both have the same denominator, or compare each with a half."

say: "Which is more: 2 1/3 pizzas or 9/4 pizzas? Mei says 9/4 because 9 is a big number."
ask: "Which is more: 2 1/3 pizzas or 9/4 pizzas? Mei says 9/4 because 9 is a big number."

2 1/3 is more. 9/4 = 2 1/4, and both have 2 wholes. A third is bigger than a quarter (sharing one pizza among 3 gives bigger slices than sharing among 4), so 2 1/3 is bigger. Mei looked at the 9 alone, but quarters are small pieces.

say: "You were real fraction explorers today: you built fractions, lined them up and compared them with good reasons."
"Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal."

p4l4-title.note: Objective: Change between improper fractions and mixed numbers using fraction bars and number lines, find a fraction of a set (and the whole set from a part) with a bar model, and compare fractions with different denominators by making the denominators the same, comparing with one half, or comparing pieces when the numerators are the same. Thinking strategies taught today: DRAW A MODEL (fraction bars, number lines, bar models), MAKE A LIST IN ORDER and COMPARE WITH A BENCHMARK (one half). Materials: paper strips (one per child, to fold into halves, quarters and eighths), paper circles to cut into quarters, 30 counters, mini whiteboards and markers. Online: before the lesson children cut out 3 paper circles and cut each into 4 equal slices; they fold paper strips on camera and write on mini whiteboards (no hold-ups to the camera). Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 2-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 24 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 24 to 32 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 32 to 35.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 35.5 to 79.5: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 35.5 to 53, check together 53 to 55.5, short teaching before page 2 55.5 to 59, page 2 on your own 59 to 77 (the last 2 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77 to 79.5. Talk time 79.5 to 84.5 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 84.5 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Draw it. Draw a picture, bar model or number line that shows what is known and what is asked. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Explain. Ask for the reason in the child's own words, said or written. Say: "How do you know? Tell it as if you were teaching a friend." Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p4l4-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 4 equal parts, and 3 of the 4 are coloured, so 3/4 of the strip. 2) 2 full cups and 1/4 of a cup left over (9/4 = 2 1/4). Four scoops make one cup: 8 scoops make 2 cups and 1 scoop is left. A GOOD REASON: Four quarters make a whole. Count the quarters in groups of 4: each group is one whole. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l4-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). More or less than a half? Point to one card at a time. Children show thumbs up (more than a half), thumbs down (less) or a flat hand (exactly a half), then you click to reveal (clicks go 3/8, 5/9, 6/12, 7/10, 2/5, 4/7). The quick test: find half of the denominator and compare it with the numerator. 3/8: half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4. 5/9: half of 9 is 4 and a half, and 5 is more. 6/12: half of 12 is 6, exactly a half. Listen for children who say "5/9 is less because 9 is big" (no follow-up question now): that idea comes back when we compare fractions later.

p4l4-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. 2) 20 ÷ 4 = 5. 3) Thirds to twelfths: multiply top and bottom by 4, so 8/12. Answers: 9, 5, 8. The other two warm-up questions (3/4 + 1/8; 1 − 3/10) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l4-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 21. Pairs use paper quarter-slices (online: cut paper circles on camera). Ask them to predict first: more than 2 pizzas or less? More than 3? Let them write the amount any way they like; listen for "eleven quarters" and "two and three quarters". Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: what if every pizza had 6 slices and they ate 11 slices? GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if each pizza had 8 slices and they ate 19? How many pizzas is that? Answer: 2 pizzas and 3 slices: 19/8 = 2 3/8.

p4l4-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 24. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather the ideas. Two debrief questions only. Write 11/4 and 2 3/4 side by side and tell children the names: 11/4 is an IMPROPER fraction (the top is bigger than the bottom, so it is more than 1); 2 3/4 is a MIXED number (a whole number and a fraction). They are the same amount. Answers: 1) 11/4 = 2 3/4. 2) 12 slices (12/4 = 3). The third question (what if each pizza had 6 slices and they ate 11? 11/6 = 1 5/6) is not asked; it is the Go further what-if on the explore slide.

p4l4-teach1.note: Teach. Strategy: DRAW A MODEL. Ask first: "Is 7/3 more or less than 1? How do you know?" (the top is bigger than the bottom). Click order: step 1, first bar fills, step 2, second bar fills, step 3, the last third, the answer. Think-aloud: "The denominator says 3 pieces make a whole. I have 7 pieces. 3 fill one bar, 3 more fill another, and 1 is left over. That is 2 and 1 third." Show the shortcut at the end: 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1; the remainder is the number of thirds left over.

p4l4-we1.note: Worked example. Children count the shaded thirds on the bars: 3, 6, 9, 12, then 13, 14. Think-aloud: "4 wholes, each cut into 3, is 12 thirds. 2 more thirds make 14 thirds." Watch for the common mistake 4 × 2 = 8 (multiplying the whole number by the numerator): have them point to 8 thirds on the bars.

p4l4-teachline.note: Teach (before Q2 of page 1, which uses quarters). Count the small jumps aloud from 0: one third, two thirds, three thirds (= 1), four thirds, five thirds, six thirds (= 2) … Click to reveal P, Q and R. Ask: "R is 8 thirds. How else can we write it?" (2 wholes and 2 thirds). "Where would 7/3 go?" (one small jump after 2).

p4l4-we2.note: Strategy: DRAW A BAR MODEL. The whole bar is ALL the stickers. The denominator tells how many equal units to cut it into; the numerator tells how many units we want. Think-aloud: "30 stickers in 5 equal units: each unit is 6. Stars are 3 units: 18." Point out that the stickers that are NOT stars are 2 units = 12. Watch for children who divide by 3 (the numerator).

p4l4-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 28 ÷ 4 = 7, 3 × 7 = 21. b) 42 ÷ 6 = 7, 5 × 7 = 35. c) 1 unit = 36 ÷ 4 = 9; she gives away 9 and keeps 3 units = 27. In c she keeps 3/4 of 36 = 27 in one step.

p4l4-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Changing a mixed number to an improper fraction by multiplying the whole number by the numerator, or forgetting to add the numerator (3 2/5 written as 6/5 or 15/5). (2) Thinking the bigger denominator means the bigger fraction (3/7 > 3/5 "because 7 is bigger than 5"). (3) Finding a fraction of a set by dividing by the numerator, or stopping at one unit (3/8 of 24 answered 8 or 3).

p4l4-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 35.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Call out: 5/4 (stand), 3/8 (sit), 6/6 (hands on head), 9/5 (stand), 7/12 (sit), 12/12 (hands on head). Then let a child call the fractions. Online: children stand and sit on camera.

p4l4-ws1.note: Minutes 35.5 to 53. Pairs do Q1 to Q3 (about 10 minutes of work). Walk around. Ask "How many pieces make one whole?" before giving any help. Q2 C is 10 quarters: children may write 2 2/4 or 2 1/2; both are right. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l4-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1c: 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 = 17 fifths. Q1d: 8 eighths in each whole, 5 × 8 = 40. Q3: glasses 3 units = 9; no glasses 5 units = 15 (or 24 − 9).

p4l4-teachcompare.note: Minutes 55.5 to 56.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). The tools are split over two slides so that each has room. Click each column: the reason, then the answer. Tool 1: change one fraction so the denominators match (2/3 = 6/9: multiply top and bottom by 3). Show it with paper strips: a strip in thirds and a strip in ninths, same length. Tool 2: compare each with a half, the "half of the denominator" test from the warm-up. Next slide: tool 3 and how to choose.

p4l4-teachcompare2.note: Minutes 56.5 to 57.5. Tool 3: same numerator, so look at the size of the pieces: sharing among 5 gives bigger pieces than sharing among 9. Then the choosing card on the right: click each line and ask the group for an example. Ask: "Which tool is quickest for 5/6 and 3/4?" (same denominator: twelfths).

p4l4-teachwhole.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5). This time we know a PART, not the whole. Draw the whole bar in 3 units and shade 2 units; the 24 goes under the shaded part, the question mark over the whole. Think-aloud: "2 units are 24, so 1 unit is 12. The bag is 3 units: 36." Watch for children who find 2/3 of 24 (= 16): ask "Is the bag bigger or smaller than the blue marbles?"

p4l4-teachfind.note: Minutes 58.5 to 59. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Strategy: MAKE A LIST IN ORDER. Change the end fractions to eighths, then list every eighth in between. The ends themselves do not count, because "between" means bigger than one and smaller than the other. The "Who am I?" riddle is now on the Think harder page (stretch 4): it uses the same idea, list everything that fits the first clues and then cross out with each new clue (example: improper fraction, denominator 4, between 1 and 2, odd numerator, closer to 2 than to 1: 5/4, 6/4, 7/4; odd: 5/4, 7/4; closer to 2: 7/4).

p4l4-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who still think a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q4 and Q5 first. Q6 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 2 minutes of this block (minute 75 to 77) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l4-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q4a: 3/4 = 6/8. b) 2/3 = 8/12. c) 4/9 is less than a half, 5/8 is more. d) Fifths are bigger pieces than sevenths. e) In twelfths: 7/12, 8/12, 10/12. Q6: 1/3 = 4/12 and 3/4 = 9/12; the ends do not count. (Who am I? is now Think harder stretch 4: 17/6, because 13/6, 15/6, 17/6 are odd, and only 17/6 is closer to 3.)

p4l4-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) Ben. 7/4 = 14/8 = 1 6/8, which is more than 1 5/8. 2) 25 (1 unit = 5, blue = 15, not blue = 5 units = 25). 3) 1/2, 7/12, 2/3, 5/6 (6/12, 7/12, 8/12, 10/12). 4) 17/6 = 2 5/6. Between 2 and 3: 13/6, 14/6, 15/6, 16/6, 17/6. Odd numerators: 13/6, 15/6, 17/6. 15/6 = 2 1/2 is exactly in the middle and 13/6 is closer to 2, so only 17/6 is closer to 3.

p4l4-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q6 and Q7. Answers: 1) 18 (half = 3 sixths, a third = 2 sixths, so 1 sixth = 3). 2) 150 pages (Monday 4 tenths, Tuesday 3 tenths, 3 tenths left = 45).

p4l4-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: In Q1, how could you cut both bars into the same size pieces? (sixths). In Q2, the rest is 3 fifths; how can we cut 3 fifths in half? (make tenths). Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l4-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: guess and check also works (try 12: 6 and 4, only 2 more; try 18: 9 and 6, 3 more). The sixths idea shows WHY: the gap between a half and a third is always one sixth. Q2: check forwards: Monday 2/5 of 150 = 60, rest 90, Tuesday 45, left 45 ✓. A common mistake is to say Tuesday is half of the whole book.

p4l4-talk.note: Minutes 79.5 to 84.5. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: 2 1/3 is more. 9/4 = 2 1/4, so both have 2 wholes; a third is bigger than a quarter (sharing a pizza among 3 gives bigger slices than among 4). Mei is a made-up character, not a child in the group: say "her idea", never name a real child. Mei looked only at the 9, but quarters are small pieces. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "Ravi says 3/7 is bigger than 3/5 because 7 is bigger than 5. What would you tell him?" (fifths are bigger pieces, so 3/5 is bigger). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l4-exit.note: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Answers: 23/5 = 4 3/5 (23 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 3). 3/5 of 25 = 15 (1 unit = 5, 3 units = 15). Extension: find a fraction between 2/3 and 3/4 (for example 17/24, because 2/3 = 16/24 and 3/4 = 18/24).

p4l4-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. HABIT: Focus habit: Explain. Ask for the reason in the child's own words, said or written. Say: "How do you know? Tell it as if you were teaching a friend." Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
